source.title_on_document: Harnessing generative AI for collaborative creativity: A study of university students’ engagement and innovation

paper_design_summary: Fifty undergraduate English majors enrolled in a communication-skills course were randomly divided into AI-supported and non-AI groups for a collaborative Alternative Uses Task about a cardboard box (PDF p. 4, sections 3.1-3.2). Students in the AI arm prompted ChatGPT-3 during ideation, and two trained raters scored fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.2-3.2.2.3). The reported tests use student counts, although the methods describe collaborative group output and do not explain the construction of individual scores (PDF p. 5, section 4.1 and Table 1).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly divided between a non-AI control condition and an AI-supported experimental condition, with 25 students per condition. Recruitment into the study was purposive; assignment to conditions is explicitly described as random. The randomization procedure is not specified.
assignment.quote: The students were then randomly divided into two groups of 25: one group performed the task without AI assistance (control group), while the other used AI (experimental group).

arms.name: Non-AI control
arms.description: Completed the cardboard-box Alternative Uses Task without AI, working face-to-face and recording responses on paper or a shared Google document (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.1). The assignment count is given in section 3.1; the analysis count is given on PDF p. 5, section 4.1.

arms.name: AI-supported (ChatGPT-3)
arms.description: Received training in ChatGPT-3 and used specific inquiries to generate and develop concepts during the identical Alternative Uses Task; instructed to distinguish AI-generated and human-written material (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2). The assignment count is given in section 3.1; the analysis count is given on PDF p. 5, section 4.1.

participants.exclusions: Exclusions and attrition are not reported. Section 3.1 describes 50 students randomly divided into groups of 25; section 4.1 reports n = 25 in each analyzed arm (PDF pp. 4-5).
participants.who: Undergraduate English majors enrolled in the Communication Skills course at the National University of Modern Languages (NUML), Islamabad, during spring 2024; 25 male and 25 female students, aged 18-22 years, recruited purposively from the same course (PDF p. 4, section 3.1).
participants.quote: An independent-samples t-test was used to assess differences in creative output between the two groups: the AI-assisted experimental group (n = 25) and the non-AI control group (n = 25).
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (journal p. 3287), section 3.1, for recruitment, demographics and randomized counts; PDF p. 5 (journal p. 3288), section 4.1, for analyzed arm counts; PDF p. 1, author affiliation 1, identifies NUML Islamabad as Pakistan.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-3 (the paper’s name; exact underlying model/version not specified)
ai_tool.how_used: After training, students directed ChatGPT-3 through specific inquiries to generate and develop ideas while completing the task; they were instructed to distinguish AI-generated and human-written contributions. Prompts, access configuration and training duration are not reported (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2; PDF p. 5, section 4.1).

task.description: Collaboratively generate multiple and varied uses for a cardboard box in the Alternative Uses Task. The control condition worked face-to-face, recording responses on paper or a shared Google document; the AI condition completed the identical task with ChatGPT-3 (PDF p. 4, sections 3.2.1-3.2.2). Subsequent reflective writing was qualitative data about the experience, not a scored creative-performance task.
task.duration: 10 minutes to collaboratively generate ideas, stated for each group in section 3.2.1; section 3.2.2 calls the AI task identical (PDF p. 4, journal p. 3287).

outcomes.name: Alternative Uses Task: fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct ideas generated in the cardboard-box Alternative Uses Task; ideas were independently scored by two trained raters using an adapted creativity rubric. PDF pp. 4-5 (journal pp. 3287-3288), section 3.2.2.3. The paper reports independent-samples t-tests with n = 25 students per arm and t(48), so participant is coded as the reported analysis unit. However, section 3.2.1 describes collaborative group output and the paper does not explain how individual scores were obtained or how group dependence was handled; the number of separately scored output records is not stated (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.1 and 4.1, Table 1).

contrasts.reported: With AI (M ± SD): 22.8 ± 5.3, n = 25; Without AI (M ± SD): 15.2 ± 4.1, n = 25; t(48) = -5.80; p < .001. The t-statistic sign is reproduced as printed; the AI arm has the higher mean.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 3288), section 4.1 and Table 1.

outcomes.name: Alternative Uses Task: flexibility
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Variety of categories represented in the cardboard-box Alternative Uses Task; ideas were independently scored by two trained raters using an adapted creativity rubric. This concerns categories within the produced ideas, not similarity between different people’s outputs. PDF pp. 4-5 (journal pp. 3287-3288), section 3.2.2.3. The paper reports independent-samples t-tests with n = 25 students per arm and t(48), so participant is coded as the reported analysis unit. However, section 3.2.1 describes collaborative group output and the paper does not explain how individual scores were obtained or how group dependence was handled; the number of separately scored output records is not stated (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.1 and 4.1, Table 1).

contrasts.reported: With AI (M ± SD): 11.6 ± 3.1, n = 25; Without AI (M ± SD): 8.4 ± 2.2, n = 25; t(48) = -4.27; p < .001. The t-statistic sign is reproduced as printed; the AI arm has the higher mean.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 3288), section 4.1 and Table 1.

outcomes.name: Alternative Uses Task: originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Novelty of Alternative Uses Task responses in comparison to a normative sample; two trained raters independently scored the ideas using a rubric adapted from creativity research. The normative sample, rating scale, and aggregation procedure are not specified. PDF pp. 4-5 (journal pp. 3287-3288), section 3.2.2.3. The paper reports independent-samples t-tests with n = 25 students per arm and t(48), so participant is coded as the reported analysis unit. However, section 3.2.1 describes collaborative group output and the paper does not explain how individual scores were obtained or how group dependence was handled; the number of separately scored output records is not stated (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.1 and 4.1, Table 1).

contrasts.reported: With AI (M ± SD): 7.9 ± 2.4, n = 25; Without AI (M ± SD): 6.1 ± 1.8, n = 25; t(48) = -3.20; p = .002. The t-statistic sign is reproduced as printed; the AI arm has the higher mean.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 3288), section 4.1 and Table 1.

outcomes.name: Alternative Uses Task: elaboration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Richness and detail in each Alternative Uses Task response; two trained raters independently scored the ideas using a rubric adapted from creativity research. The rating scale and aggregation procedure are not specified. PDF pp. 4-5 (journal pp. 3287-3288), section 3.2.2.3. The paper reports independent-samples t-tests with n = 25 students per arm and t(48), so participant is coded as the reported analysis unit. However, section 3.2.1 describes collaborative group output and the paper does not explain how individual scores were obtained or how group dependence was handled; the number of separately scored output records is not stated (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.1 and 4.1, Table 1).

contrasts.reported: With AI (M ± SD): 24.5 ± 6.9, n = 25; Without AI (M ± SD): 18.3 ± 5.7, n = 25; t(48) = -3.90; p < .001. The t-statistic sign is reproduced as printed; the AI arm has the higher mean.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is reported. The author affiliations are educational institutions; the funding statement reports no specific financial support and the authors declare no competing interests. OpenAI is identified as the developer of the tool, not as a research partner.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (journal p. 3284), affiliations, Funding and Competing Interests; PDF p. 4 (journal p. 3287), section 3.2.2.

eligibility.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly reports random division of students between AI and non-AI conditions (PDF p. 4, journal p. 3287). The study reports 50 students and n = 25 in each analyzed arm, meeting the threshold exactly (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.1 and 4.1). Four divergent-thinking dimensions are scored on AUT outputs by trained raters while AI is available in the experimental arm (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.2-3.2.2.3 and Table 1). Collaborative production versus apparent participant-level analysis is unresolved and requires clarification before treating the reported precision as based on independent people.

one_line_finding: The AI-supported arm had higher mean fluency (22.8 vs. 15.2), flexibility (11.6 vs. 8.4), originality (7.9 vs. 6.1), and elaboration (24.5 vs. 18.3) than the non-AI arm (PDF p. 5, journal p. 3288, Table 1).
open_questions: Section 3.2.1 describes each group of 25 collaborating, but section 4.1 reports n = 25 per arm and Table 1 reports t(48). Were outputs and creativity scores separately recorded for individuals, or were shared team scores attributed to students, and how was dependence within groups handled? (PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.2.1 and 4.1, Table 1.)

Was this structured face-to-face AUT experiment conducted in a separate supervised research session or integrated into ordinary coursework? The paper identifies course enrollment but does not state this distinction; lab_rct is used for the reported experimental task (PDF p. 4, sections 3.1-3.2).

What were the scoring rubric, normative sample, score aggregation rules and numerical inter-rater reliability? The paper says Cohen’s kappa was calculated but reports no value and does not supply these scoring details (PDF pp. 4-5, section 3.2.2.3).

The qualitative results describe reflections from fifty students who used ChatGPT-3, whereas the experimental methods allocate only 25 students to AI. The qualitative denominator and any additional AI exposure are unclear; the quantitative analysis counts are taken from section 4.1 (PDF p. 7, text below Figure 2, versus PDF pp. 4-5, sections 3.1 and 4.1).
notes: Read the complete markdown, including the references through the final page; no appendix or supplement is mentioned. Verified PDF pages 1, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 13, and recovered Table 1 with PyMuPDF find_tables. Locators give one-based PDF pages and, where useful, printed journal pages. lab_rct denotes the structured face-to-face experimental task; the physical venue and whether it was ordinary coursework are not specified. Outcome unit is coded participant to reflect the reported t-tests, not as confirmation of independent individual production; n_units remains null because separately scored output/team records are not enumerated. The four scored AUT dimensions are the eligible outcomes. Qualitative reports of apprehension, fixation and role ambiguity are not scored creativity or between-person similarity measures and are not entered as outcomes; post-task reflections do not establish an after_ai outcome. No across_people or delayed unassisted performance outcome is reported. No primary outcome, preregistration, participant overlap with another paper, or data/code link is reported. No effect sizes or other unprinted statistics were computed.
